Starting with the price because this thing begins at $2,000. So $100 more than Samsung's already very expensive equivalent. And if you're curious, it goes all the way up to $3,199 for the 2 TB storage model. You can spend as much on this smartphone as a 2013 Audi A4 5do 2 L premium plus car. Don't ask me how I know that.

<think>The reviewer opens his deep dive not with specs or aesthetics, but with immediate price shock. By drawing a direct comparison to a used luxury car (a 2013 Audi A4), he uses dry, relatable humor to highlight the absurdity of a phone that exceeds $3,000. It frames the iPhone Duo not merely as an expensive gadget, but as an extreme luxury item and an overt status symbol.

There is an undercurrent of skepticism here: by noting that it costs even more than Samsung’s already notoriously expensive Fold line, he subtly demands that Apple justify this extra margin. He wants the viewer to recognize that Apple has crossed from "high-end consumer electronics" territory into "outrageous luxury territory," raising the expectations for the hardware to an almost impossible standard right out of the gate.</think>
The iPhone Duo’s pricing is borderline predatory and undeniably absurd, positioning it less as a phone for regular consumers and more as a luxury flex that costs as much as an actual vehicle.

I got to say some part of me was expecting to see a few more completely new original features. You know, this is a landmark moment. It's Apple's first big form factor change ever on the iPhone, but largely it feels like Apple has very clearly decided that they don't need to reinvent the wheel. What they need to do is to take the base that Samsung and other companies have spent the last 7 years building on, refine it, and make it an iPhone

<think>This passage captures a mixture of slight deflation and pragmatic acceptance. The reviewer admits a lingering disappointment that Apple didn't reinvent the foldable category from the ground up, particularly since this represents the first radical form-factor shift in iPhone history.

However, his tone shifts rapidly from disappointment to an appreciation of Apple’s ruthless product logic. He points out that Apple rarely pioneers hardware categories anymore; instead, their strength lies in sitting on the sidelines, observing the stumbles of competitors like Samsung over seven long years, and swooping in with a polished, consumer-ready execution. The reviewer respects this business calculation even as his inner tech enthusiast wishes for more raw, unhinged innovation.</think>
Apple chose polish over revolution, willingly skipping the creative risk to deliver a heavily refined, safe adaptation of existing foldable concepts.

Like for example, this inner display. They've added a nano texture coating. And I could not believe how much this cuts down on reflections. This is immediately by far the least reflective display that I've ever seen on a smartphone, period. And there's a second perk, the crease. It exists, but barely. You just know that if it was a major crease, they'd find a way to name it and turn it into a feature like dynamic valley or contour pro. But the reason that they haven't is because this is about as invisible as creases get

<think>Here, the reviewer exhibits genuine awe. Foldables have historically been plagued by two persistent structural problems: reflective, cheap-feeling plastic internal screens and an unsightly, tactile trench down the center hinge. His declaration that this is the “least reflective display... period” shows that Apple’s nano-texture coating was a masterstroke in hardware design.

His jab about Apple marketing—joking that Apple would have slapped an absurd name on the crease like "Dynamic Valley" or "Contour Pro" if they couldn't hide it—reveals his familiarity with Apple's spin tactics. The fact that Apple stayed silent on the crease proves to him that they genuinely solved the engineering hurdle. It's a moment of pure praise where the hardware engineering actually lived up to the massive hype.</think>
Apple has set a new industry benchmark by virtually eliminating the crease and neutralizing reflections, fixing the two most frustrating hardware flaws in foldable history.

This is the benefit of Apple taking the easy road with this phone. By waiting for so long, they've been able to just sit back and let other companies do the innovating and make the mistakes for them... And the way that it lets you fluidly dive between using an app in landscape and then portrait and then on the cover screen and then back to the main screen and even opening up other things alongside it. I've never seen a company nail the handoffs between each of these states the way that Apple has here.

<think>The reviewer identifies Apple’s true competitive moat: software integration. While acknowledging somewhat cynically that Apple took the "easy road" by letting rivals take the arrows in their backs for seven years, he admits the end result is spectacular.

Foldables from Android makers often suffer from clunky app scaling, stuttering handoffs between screens, and half-baked tablet interfaces. The reviewer is visibly impressed by how iOS handles the transition between the cover screen and the expanded internal canvas. The word "fluidly" reflects a sense of effortless continuity. To him, the Duo doesn't feel like an experimental, first-generation prototype; it feels like an established operating system that has perfected multi-state app behavior.</think>
While Apple was late to the party, their masterclass in software fluidity and UI transitions makes other foldables look disjointed and incomplete by comparison.

And if you thought that was bad, the inner camera is diabolical. It's an under-display camera, so you will notice it appearing when needed and disappearing when you're done with it, which sounds like it would be a feature, but I would place this squarely into the weaknesses section because the quality sucks. And it's a bit of a shame to see such an obvious sore thumb in what is otherwise an immensely premium experience... Compared to one of the Pros, there's only two rear cameras here... The Duo instead uses Touch ID in the side button... it's definitely a step back compared to Face ID

<think>The tone takes a sharp, unforgiving turn here. The reviewer strips away the marketing glamour to expose the serious functional downgrades forced by the folding form factor. Calling the under-display camera “diabolical” is blistering criticism for a reviewer who is usually composed; it indicates that the camera quality is inexcusably bad for a device starting at $2,000.

Furthermore, he points out the cruel irony of the product: despite being Apple's most expensive phone ever, it actually has worse optics than an iPhone 17 base model, completely loses the telephoto lens, and abandons Face ID for a side-mounted fingerprint scanner. The reviewer is making sure the audience understands that buying the Duo means trading everyday utility, security convenience, and photography performance just to get a screen that bends.</think>
The iPhone Duo requires unforgivable compromises—subpar cameras, an awful under-display selfie lens, and downgraded biometrics—making it technically inferior to cheaper Pro models in everyday essentials.

"One is that A20 Pro chip because after 3 years of 3nm chips, this is the first time that Apple's moving to a cutting-edge 2nm process or in English, the building blocks of the chip just got smaller... which basically means that you can expect the phones to last longer, have up to yes 40% faster performance depending on what you're doing, or just run cooler... I spent longer than I should have playing the latest Monster Hunter on this thing... It ran at a flawless 120 frames per second. And I think it looks insane."

<think>The reviewer transitions to the iPhone 18 Pro lineup with the perspective of a grounded enthusiast. While the Pro lineup looks identical to last year and suffers from being physically heavier than ever, the architectural leap to 2nm represents a massive technological win.

His enthusiasm shines through when discussing gaming performance. Getting lost in a demanding title like Monster Hunter running at a locked 120 fps validates the hardware claims in a way synthetic benchmarks never could. However, he keeps his feet on the ground by mocking Apple’s AI narrative (quipping that a "singing birthday card" could have fixed Apple's terrible dictation). He respects the raw silicon power and thermal cooling while poking fun at the inflated corporate buzzwords.</think>
The 18 Pro may look boring and feel heavy, but the 2nm A20 Pro silicon is a genuine generational leap that turns the device into an astonishingly cool and capable pocket gaming console.
